demo_steps.title: Five discrete positions
demo_steps.narration: The five identical frustum glyphs and red arrows show the camera translating laterally — motion parallel to the image plane, perpendicular to the optical axis. The frustum orientation stays fixed.

demo_steps.title: Continuous translation
demo_steps.narration: Slide the active camera along the path. It passes through the five reference positions without rotating — pure lateral translation means zero change in viewing direction.

demo_steps.title: Depth-dependent parallax
demo_steps.narration: With parallax mode on, the near point (orange) projects to a position that shifts more on the image plane than the far point (blue) for the same lateral camera displacement — apparent motion is inversely proportional to depth.

demo_steps.title: Full traversal
demo_steps.narration: At the rightmost position the shift arrows are longest. The ratio of near-to-far shift equals the ratio of far-to-near depth, confirming the 1/Z scaling of lateral image motion.

plan.geometry_notes: Layout is a horizontal strip, total width ~10 world units, height ~3 units. Five camera glyphs centered at x = -4, -2, 0, +2, +4, all at y = 0 baseline. Each glyph: apex dot (black sphere r=0.08) at (x, 0, 0); image-plane rectangle centered at (x, 1.1, 0) with width 0.9 and height 0.6; four frustum edges from apex to rectangle corners; two diagonals crossing the rectangle. All edges black #000000, line thickness ~2px. Six red arrows #dd0000 at y = -0.35, centered at x = -5, -3, -1, +1, +3, +5, each ~0.8 units long with a triangular arrowhead pointing +X. Active camera glyph highlighted with edges in #333333 and apex in #222222, slightly thicker. Ghost positions shown as thin grey #aaaaaa outlines. Parallax mode: near point orange #ff8800 at (activeX, 2.8, 0) representing a point at depth Z=2; far point blue #1a66cc at (activeX, 3.5, 0) representing depth Z=5. Image-plane shift arrow length = k * displacement / depth, with k=0.4. Shift arrows drawn on the image plane of the active camera, horizontal, colored to match their scene point. White background #ffffff throughout.
plan.notes: This is a flat 2D diagram (axis_screen_angles: null). Render all frustum edges as THREE.Line or Line2 with consistent thickness. The five reference frustums are static; the active camera is a separate group that translates along X driven by the slider. Ghost trail: when the slider moves, leave thin grey copies at integer positions already passed. Parallax elements (scene points, projection lines, shift arrows) are in a separate group toggled by showParallax — hidden by default to match the clean source appearance. Arrowheads are small filled triangles (ShapeGeometry). No perspective camera needed; use OrthographicCamera for the flat look.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a horizontal strip in which the same wireframe camera appears five times, evenly spaced across a white field and interleaved with thick red arrows. Each camera is a viewing frustum seen from behind and slightly below: a solid black dot at the bottom marks the projection center, four straight edges rise from it to the corners of a wide rectangle standing for the image plane, and lines cross that rectangle to its lower corners, so the pyramid reads as pointing up and away from the viewer. The five copies match exactly in size and orientation. Red arrows run horizontally along the base of the strip, one before the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, and one trailing off the right edge, every arrowhead pointing right. Because the frusta aim away from the viewer while the arrows travel across the picture, the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it. The sequence illustrates sideways camera motion parallel to the image plane, as when a scene slides past the side window of a moving car, in which the forward velocity component is zero.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for sliding the camera sideways parallel to the image plane; the frustum translates across the strip while projected scene points shift laterally, showing motion with zero forward component.
- Slider for lateral displacement; the active camera moves from left to right and image-plane vectors lengthen with the displacement, making the relation between side motion and apparent image shift explicit.
- Toggle between the 3-D path and projected optical flow for near versus far points; the flow view shows larger shifts for nearer points, connecting lateral translation to depth-dependent parallax.
authoredContext:
Consider a camera translating laterally, as shown in
the figure. This will happen if you are looking
through a side window of a car at the scene passing by. In this case,
the forward velocity is zero, $V_Z=0$.

Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.

interactions.label: Lateral displacement
interactions.teaches: Dragging the camera sideways parallel to the image plane shifts every projected scene point laterally, and the on-image shift vectors lengthen in proportion to the displacement — side motion produces pure lateral image motion with zero forward component

interactions.label: Slide camera sideways
interactions.teaches: Watching the frustum translate across the strip while the projected points slide the opposite way makes the perpendicular-to-line-of-sight motion concrete, like scenery passing a car's side window

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the optical-flow view reveals that the nearer point's flow arrow is longer than the farther point's — lateral translation yields depth-dependent parallax, the cue that lets motion reveal depth

demo_steps.title: Camera at rest
demo_steps.narration: With zero lateral displacement the projected near and far points sit at their baseline image positions and the shift vectors vanish. The frustum aims up-and-away; the red arrows mark the upcoming sideways direction.

demo_steps.title: Translate sideways
demo_steps.narration: Slide the camera to the right. Both projected points move left on the image plane and the shift vectors grow with the displacement, while the rays keep zero forward component.

demo_steps.title: Depth-dependent parallax
demo_steps.narration: In the optical-flow view the near point's horizontal flow arrow is clearly longer than the far point's for the same camera displacement — apparent image speed is inversely proportional to depth.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Build one camera rig in a local frame and translate it along +X (screen-right, the red-arrow direction). Apex/projection-center sphere radius ~0.09 at local (0,0,0), black #000000. Image-plane rectangle centered ~ (0, 1.35, 0.7), width ~2.2 in X and ~1.1 along its tilted vertical, drawn as 4 black edges; 4 frustum edges from apex to the rectangle corners; 2 diagonals across the rectangle (top-left to bottom-right and top-right to bottom-left) so the pyramid reads pointing up-and-away. Optical axis points up-and-away (~+Y and +Z). Near scene point orange #ff8800 at world (0.7, 3.0, 2.2); far scene point blue #1a66cc at world (0.7, 6.0, 5.0); both have the same lateral world offset so parallax is purely from depth. Projected image points computed by intersecting the apex->point ray with the image plane; lateral shift vector on the image plane = projected(d) - projected(0), scaled for visibility. Red arrows #e00000 as ~6 cone+shaft meshes spaced ~1.6 units along X at y ~ -0.45, all pointing +X. Optical-flow view: front-on plane, flow arrow length = k * lateralDisp / depth with k ~ 0.6, near arrow visibly longer than far. Whole scene fits X in [-4, 4], Y in [-0.6, 2.2], Z in [0, 6].
interactionPlan.notes: Recompute projected image points, shift vectors, and projection rays reactively on every slider/animation frame; the animation should drive the same lateralDisp value the slider exposes (loop a 0->3->0 sweep). For the toggle, keep both the 3D rig group and a separate front-on optical-flow group in the scene and show/hide rather than rebuilding geometry. Render frustum edges and diagonals as LineSegments with linewidth via a thin cylinder/Line2 fallback for crispness; keep the apex sphere and scene-point spheres as MeshStandardMaterial for depth cues.
